title: Baking Cups From China Fail Taiwan Safety Tests at the Border
summaryZh: 中國製烘焙紙杯等食品器具邊境檢驗不合格，食藥署啟動逐批查驗。
summaryHi: चीन से आए बेकिंग कप ताइवान की सीमा पर सुरक्षा जाँच में फेल हुए।
summaryEs: Moldes de papel para hornear de China no superan los controles de Taiwán.
summaryJa: 中国製の紙製ベーキングカップなどが台湾の水際検査で不合格に。
summaryKo: 중국산 종이 베이킹컵 등이 대만 국경 안전검사에서 불합격했다.
summaryEn: Paper baking cups and kitchen tools from China failed Taiwan's border safety tests.
paragraphs: Taiwan's Food and Drug Administration (TFDA) announced on Tuesday that several shipments of food-contact products made in China had been intercepted at the border after failing safety checks known as dissolution tests.

These tests measure how much residue a container or utensil releases when it touches food. Two batches of paper baking cups imported by DFI Home Furnishings, which operates Ikea in Taiwan, recorded 217 and 226 parts per million, far above the legal limit of 30.

A shipment of baking paper registered 67 ppm, while a batch of kitchen tools reached 123 ppm. Liu Fang-ming, a TFDA director, said the products would be returned or destroyed. The kitchen tool importer will also face inspection rates of 20 to 50 percent.

Over the six months to October 12, 11 of 206 batches of Chinese paper utensils with plastic-coated surfaces failed, a failure rate of 5.3 percent. In response, the agency will inspect every such batch from October 20 to November 19.
Other rejected imports included durian from Vietnam, bok choy from Indonesia and radishes from China, which contained excessive pesticides, sweeteners, bleaching agents or heavy metals.
Taiwan checks food products at its border. On Tuesday, the Food and Drug Administration said some products from China were not safe.
Two boxes of paper baking cups did not pass the test. They came for Ikea in Taiwan. The safe limit is 30. These cups had 217 and 226.
Some baking paper and some kitchen tools also failed. All of these products will go back or be destroyed.
From April to October, 11 out of 206 groups of these paper products failed. So now Taiwan will check every group from China until November 19.
Some foods were also stopped, like durian from Vietnam and bok choy from Indonesia. They had too many chemicals in them.
Taiwan's Food and Drug Administration (TFDA) said on Tuesday that several shipments of kitchen products from China had been stopped at the border because they failed safety tests.

The tests check how much material can come out of a product and get into food. Two batches of paper baking cups, imported by the company that runs Ikea in Taiwan, showed levels of 217 and 226 parts per million. The legal limit is only 30. This means the cups were more than seven times over the limit.
A batch of baking paper reached 67, and a batch of kitchen tools reached 123. An official said all three shipments would be sent back or destroyed.
Between April and October, 11 of 206 batches of these paper products from China failed, a rate of about 5 percent. Because of this, the TFDA will check every batch from October 20 to November 19.
Several foods were also rejected, including durian from Vietnam and radishes from China, because they contained too many pesticides or other chemicals.

Taiwan's Food and Drug Administration (TFDA) announced on Tuesday that several shipments of food-contact products made in China had been intercepted at the border after failing safety checks known as dissolution tests.

These tests measure how much residue a container or utensil releases when it touches food. Two batches of paper baking cups imported by DFI Home Furnishings, which operates Ikea in Taiwan, recorded 217 and 226 parts per million, far above the legal limit of 30.

A shipment of baking paper registered 67 ppm, while a batch of kitchen tools reached 123 ppm. Liu Fang-ming, a TFDA director, said the products would be returned or destroyed. The kitchen tool importer will also face inspection rates of 20 to 50 percent.

Over the six months to October 12, 11 of 206 batches of Chinese paper utensils with plastic-coated surfaces failed, a failure rate of 5.3 percent. In response, the agency will inspect every such batch from October 20 to November 19.
Other rejected imports included durian from Vietnam, bok choy from Indonesia and radishes from China, which contained excessive pesticides, sweeteners, bleaching agents or heavy metals.

Taiwan's Food and Drug Administration (TFDA) disclosed on Tuesday that a number of Chinese-made food-contact products, ranging from kitchen tools to paper baking cups and baking paper, had been intercepted at the border after failing dissolution tests.

Such tests gauge how much residue leaches out of a utensil or container into the food it holds. Two consignments of baking cups imported by DFI Home Furnishings, the operator of Ikea in Taiwan, registered evaporation residues of 217 and 226 ppm, more than seven times the statutory ceiling of 30 ppm.

Baking paper and a batch of kitchen tools were also found to exceed the limit, at 67 and 123 ppm respectively. According to Liu Fang-ming of the TFDA, the goods will be either returned or destroyed, and the tool importer will be subject to inspection rates of up to 50 percent.

The crackdown follows a worrying pattern: between April and mid-October, 11 of 206 batches of plastic-coated paper utensils from China failed, a rate of 5.3 percent. Consequently, the agency has introduced batch-by-batch checks until November 19.
Food imports were caught too, with durian, bok choy and radishes among items rejected for excessive pesticides, sweeteners, bleaching agents or heavy metals.

Taiwan's Food and Drug Administration (TFDA) revealed on Tuesday that several consignments of Chinese-manufactured food-contact goods, including kitchen implements, paper baking cups and baking paper, had been intercepted at the border for failing mandatory dissolution tests.

These assessments quantify the residue that migrates from a utensil into food. Most strikingly, two batches of baking cups imported by DFI Home Furnishings, which runs Ikea's Taiwanese stores, contained 217 and 226 ppm of evaporation residue, vastly exceeding the statutory threshold of 30 ppm.

Baking paper and kitchen tools likewise breached the limit, at 67 and 123 ppm respectively. Liu Fang-ming, a senior TFDA official, confirmed that the products would be returned or destroyed, while the tool importer now faces inspection rates of between 20 and 50 percent.

Crucially, the incident is not isolated. From April to mid-October, 11 of 206 batches of plastic-coated paper utensils from China failed, a non-compliance rate of 5.3 percent, prompting the agency to impose comprehensive batch-by-batch inspections until November 19.

Several foodstuffs, among them durian, bok choy and radishes, were also rejected for containing excessive pesticides, sweeteners, bleaching agents or heavy metals, underlining the scale of the screening effort.
